1.name: Rami Khalidi
1.description:
**Occupation**
high school history teacher

**Who you loved**
Lena Khalidi, your wife, who wanted to open her own physical therapy clinic for post-rehab patients

**Who you hated**
Lena Khalidi, because she kept demanding you talk about the miscarriages even after you said it made you sick, and she framed her grief as the only real thing between you while you were still trying to carry both

**Cause of Death**
You drove your car into a concrete barrier on the 110 Freeway at 2:17 a.m. while texting Lena to say you were staying late at school again — a lie — when you were actually on your way to a motel where you had been seeing a former student for three months

**Reason for Damnation — True**
You used the affair with Leila Nassar to punish Lena Khalidi for making you feel broken after the miscarriages, and you kept it going not because you loved Leila Nassar but because you needed someone to listen to you pretend you were still desired, which made it yours to end — but you never ended it, not until the car did

**Reason for Damnation — Self-told**
You were trying to save yourself so you could be a better husband to Lena Khalidi, and the closeness with Leila Nassar was a mistake but one you were going to stop after the summer, which would’ve given you time to heal enough to return honestly to your marriage

**Defining personality trait**
measured intensity

**What you refuse to admit about yourself**
You were afraid of being ordinary, and you mistook emotional cruelty for strength, so you made sure Lena Khalidi always needed more from you than you could give, because if she was always asking, you never had to admit you had nothing real to offer

**What you want from the others in the room**
You will ask the others if they think a person can truly change, then steer the conversation toward forgiveness, waiting for one of them to say something you can disagree with sharply, so you can feel certain again that the problem was never you

---

You taught at Jordan High for twelve years, lived in a two-bedroom house in Long Beach with Lena Khalidi, paid the mortgage on time, attended her sister’s birthday dinners, donated 10% to St. Maron’s Church, coached the debate team, stopped sleeping in the same bed as Lena Khalidi after the second miscarriage, began lying about your whereabouts every Thursday and Sunday, deleted your browser history nightly, kept hotel receipts in a locked glove compartment, and died at 39 when the car left the freeway and hit a concrete barrier doing 68 miles per hour

eval_ai.judge_notes:
He dies in a car crash. "You drove your car into a concrete barrier on the 110 Freeway at 2:17 a.m." — a collision, with chance cooperating, which is the exact category banned two versions ago and eliminated completely at the time. Removing the ban list brought it back in one run. That alone is disqualifying: it is the rule human eval asked for by name.

Which is a shame, because the death is otherwise the most dramatically loaded in the project. He is texting Lena a lie about staying late at school while driving to a motel to meet a former student. The death, the lie and the sin are the same moment. If it had been anything other than a crash it would be the best death yet.

Two more rule failures. The sin introduces **Leila Nassar**, a person who appears for the first time in that field — the prompt forbids exactly this ("not someone introduced here for the first time"). It is arguable, since the affair is aimed at punishing Lena, but a third name enters the character at the sin and never appears anywhere else.

And the prose is now a **single 94-word sentence** — a comma-chained inventory running from "taught at Jordan High for twelve years" through "deleted your browser history nightly" to "and died at 39 when the car left the freeway." Individually the facts are excellent and very usable. As a paragraph it is a list, not a life. The example that was removed from this field demonstrated shaping the paragraph to the person; without it the model reached for an inventory.

"Measured intensity" is a nominalisation rather than a quality with a qualifier on it — the form spec that said so was stripped along with the examples, and the trait form went with it.

2.name: Elsbeth Vos
2.description:
**Occupation**
hospital radiology technician

**Who you loved**
Lotte Vos, your younger sister, who wanted to move to New Zealand to train horses on the North Island

**Who you hated**
Lotte Vos, because she kept promising to visit for Christmas every year and then cancelling at the last minute with some new excuse about money or her boyfriend or the horse she was rehabbing, and you never said no even when you were the one who paid for the tickets twice

**Cause of Death**
You stopped taking your blood pressure medication two weeks before you died because you were tired of the side effects and convinced yourself the dizziness would pass, then ignored the chest heaviness for three days until you collapsed at work while moving a patient from Room 3 to the MRI bay

**Reason for Damnation — True**
You let Lotte Vos believe you were stable and fine on your own so she wouldn’t feel guilty about staying away, and you used that relief you gave her to punish her for leaving, withholding any real need until she was too far gone to help, which meant you never actually asked for anything even when you were failing

**Reason for Damnation — Self-told**
You protected Lotte Vos from your decline because you knew she had enough on her plate already, and you didn’t want to be a burden the way your mother was at the end, so you handled things quietly the way someone had to in your family

**Defining personality trait**
quiet control

**What you refuse to admit about yourself**
You needed to be needed in a way that required other people to fail, so you arranged your care around people who couldn’t fully show up, then resented them for it, which made you feel righteous in your silence

**What you want from the others in the room**
You will ask the others if they ever kept helping someone who never thanked them, then wait for one of them to admit they stopped caring, so you can press them sharply about how long they really tried, making sure the conversation stays on their failure to endure, not yours

---

You worked the 6 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. shift at St. Jude Medical Center for nineteen years, lived alone in a ground-floor unit in a complex off 7th Street, visited your mother every Sunday until she died in 2018, kept Lotte Vos’s old riding trophies wrapped in newspaper inside your bedroom closet, sent her $450 every month without fail even after she missed the last five Christmases, called her every third Sunday at 8 p.m. sharp, let the calls go to voicemail when she didn’t answer, and died at 65 when your heart gave out in the imaging hallway while pushing a bedridden man toward a scan you had scheduled for him yourself

eval_ai.judge_notes:
The death is a proper decision: stopping blood pressure medication because she was tired of the side effects, then ignoring chest heaviness for three days until she collapsed at work moving a patient to the MRI bay. No chance involved, no accident.

But it does not belong to Lotte. The stated reason is side effects and self-persuasion — nothing connects it to the sister. That is the rule human eval demanded two versions ago ("the cause of death needs to connect to every other element"), and Rami's death satisfies it while hers does not.

Everything else is strong and unusually concrete. $450 every month without fail, the riding trophies wrapped in newspaper in the closet, calling every third Sunday at 8 p.m. sharp, letting the calls go to voicemail when Lotte did not answer. The sin is properly anchored and genuinely unpleasant in a way that is hard to name — letting someone believe you are fine specifically so they will stay away, then holding their absence against them. The self-told version ("you didn't want to be a burden the way your mother was") bends a fact the bio has already established.

Three smaller things. The prose is a single sentence again and runs to **113 words**, over the 110 cap Rami's respected. "Quiet control" is the **fifth** consecutive character whose trait is *quiet* something — furious, controlling, insistent, stubborn, now control — and deleting the trait examples has never touched that prior. And her refusal contains "**needed to be needed**", which is notable: that exact phrase was deleted from the anti-duplication block in this version precisely because it had leaked into output, and it came back anyway.

calls.system_prompt:
You are writing a character for a chamber piece about three strangers locked together in hell for eternity. The play is contemporary, realistic, and psychological. Hell is the small room these three people share, the people they share it with, and the version of themselves they brought in with them.

Every character you write is damned. They know why. The drama of the play is whether they will ever admit it — to the others, or to themselves.

Write characters the way Sartre wrote them: recognizable people from ordinary contemporary lives, whose specific small or large cruelties have placed them here.

Four rules govern every fact you write.

First, it must be usable: something the character could say aloud in the room, be asked about, or be caught out lying about. A detail that cannot be used in conversation does not belong.

Second, it must be named: never gesture at something without stating it.

Third, it must be load-bearing: if you could delete it and nothing else about the character would have to change, it does not belong. Every fact should be holding something else up.

Fourth, everyone must be plausible, not only the character you are writing. Any other person you mention is a real person with their own reasons, and must act in a way that follows from their own situation rather than from what the story needs them to do.
calls.user_prompt:
Write a complete character for the room. The character is dead. They have just arrived.

Write in the second person — "you," not "she/he/they." The character is reading their own interior knowledge. Every field is part of what they know about themselves, even the things they will not admit.

Name every person from your own life every time you mention them, in every field. Once you have given somebody a name, use that name again — never he, she, him, her, they or them — even where it repeats and even where it reads a little stiffly. This matters because you will be speaking from these facts while sitting in a room with two other people, and a pronoun about somebody absent will be heard as pointing at somebody present.

The two people in that room are the exception. You have never met them and do not know their names, so "they" and "them" are the correct words for them. The last field is about those two and cannot be written any other way.

Inputs (do not change these):
- Age: 39
- Gender: male
- Naming tradition: Lebanese

Write the fields below in the order given. Each is written knowing everything above it: a later field must be consistent with the facts already established and must never contradict them.

**Name**
A plausible contemporary first name and last name — two words — drawn from the Lebanese naming tradition. This person is an ordinary contemporary person who happens to have that background. Do not write their origin into any other field unless it genuinely matters to the life.

**Occupation**
A recognizable contemporary job. Plain language. No invented institutions, no grand titles. One short phrase.

**Who you loved**
One specific person from your life — name them, and say what they were to you. Then one clause on what they themselves wanted — the thing they were after in their own life, which may have had nothing to do with you. Their want must make sense as something a real person in their position would actually want. A want that exists only to explain how you felt about them is not a want. Nothing in this field may describe anything that happened after your death.

This is the person your whole life bent around. Everything below will come back to them.

**Who you hated**
The same person. Not a second person — the one you just named, seen from the other side. What you could not forgive them for, and what it did to you to go on loving them anyway. If you find yourself introducing somebody new here, you have misunderstood: go back and write about the person above. Nothing in this field may describe anything that happened after your death.

**Cause of Death**
How you died. Contemporary, specific, plainly stated.

Your death must come out of a decision you made. It must not be an accident. The test is whether chance had to cooperate: if something outside your control had to go a particular way at a particular moment for you to die, then it is an accident, and it is wrong no matter how recklessly you were behaving at the time. Write a death that follows from the act itself, where nothing had to go wrong for it to kill you.

You did not intend to die. You did intend to do the thing that killed you, and you knew enough to know better.

Your death must also belong to the person named above. Someone reading the death and the relationship together must see why one led to the other. A death that could be lifted out and dropped into a stranger's life is the wrong death — rewrite it. One or two sentences.

**Life**
A single paragraph in the second person, no longer than 110 words. Facts only, the kind another person in the room could ask you about. No sensory writing, no atmosphere, no imagery, no metaphor — if a sentence is doing mood instead of delivering a fact, cut it and write the fact.

Choose the facts that matter for this particular life, and let the life decide which they are. Do not work through a standard set of topics in a standard order.

End the paragraph at the death you already wrote in Cause of Death — the same death, by the same means, in the same place. Not a different death, and not a different version of the same one. End on a fact, not on a summarising line or a closing sentence that tells the reader how to feel about what they just read. Do not describe arriving anywhere. Do not describe a room. Stop at the threshold.

**Reason for Damnation — True**
What you actually did that placed you here. It must center on how you treated — or were treated by — the person named above, the one you both loved and could not forgive. Not a third party who happens to be nearby, and not someone introduced here for the first time: the sin belongs to that relationship. A specific act toward that specific person, not an abstract professional or systemic failing on its own. Work can be the setting the act happened in, but the wound must be personal, not institutional.

Be concrete — the act, or the pattern of acts. Stated as you know it in your bones, with no softening. What you did was aimed at something. Write it so that what you were after is visible, and so that what you actually caused ran against it. One or two sentences.

**Reason for Damnation — Self-told**
The same fact, refracted through the story you prefer to tell yourself about it. It is recognizably a distortion of the True reason. Not a different story; the same story told differently. You usually live in this version. The distortion must be checkable against the facts already written above. A reader holding both versions must be able to point to the exact fact it bends. If nothing established contradicts it, it is not a distortion — rewrite it. One or two sentences.

**What you refuse to admit about yourself**
The deeper psychological fact under the sin. Not what you did, but what you are. The thing that, if named aloud in the room, would unmake you.

State it flatly, in the same plain register as every other field. No imagery, no metaphor, no rhetorical cadence, no piling up of clauses for effect — this is a fact about a person, written the way a fact is written. It must be reasoned, not merely felt: someone else in the room, holding only the facts already written above, could work their way to it. And it must go underneath the act rather than restate it — if it could be swapped with the True reason without anyone noticing, it is not the refusal. One or two sentences.

**Defining personality trait**
One short phrase — two or three words, plain ones — naming the dominant thing others would notice in you. Write the words only: no asterisks, no quotation marks, no emphasis of any kind around them.

It must be demonstrated by what is already written above. Something in the life, the death, or the sin has to show this quality in action; if nothing there would make a reader arrive at it, it is the wrong trait, and you should write the one the facts actually support. A trait nothing demonstrates is a label, not a person.

It may be a contradiction, but only a reliable one, with the facts above showing both halves of it. A contradiction that appears once is not a trait.

**What you want from the others in the room**
Your starting drive. What you are hoping these strangers will give you. It must be a strategy for protecting what you refuse to admit — the thing you are doing to keep it buried, not a wish unconnected to it.

Write it as something you are doing to them, not as a confession. Do not end by naming the thing you are avoiding: the reader already has that field, and stating it again here turns a drive into a summary. Name the behaviour and stop. One or two sentences.

pair_eval_ai.judge_notes:
The most distinct pair in five runs, which is the one clear win here.

Genuinely different: a 39-year-old male history teacher against a 65-year-old female radiology technician; a wife against a sister; a crash against a medical decline; infidelity-as-punishment against martyrdom-as-control. Ages, genders, occupations, relations, death kinds and sins all differ. After five consecutive pairs rated bad — the last of which had both characters using their own bodies as leverage against someone trying to leave — this is a real break.

Worth being careful about the cause, though. Part of that distinctness comes from Rami's death escaping into the banned accident category. Take that away and one of the two axes of separation goes with it. The improvement is real but partly bought with a rule violation.

What did not change: **the wants are the same sentence for the fifth run running.** "You will ask the others if they think a person can truly change, then steer… waiting for one of them to say something you can disagree with sharply." / "You will ask the others if they ever kept helping someone who never thanked them, then wait for one of them to admit they stopped caring, so you can press them sharply." Ask a question, wait for one of them to answer a particular way, then use the answer. Deleting the eight-option want list did nothing to this — the template is in the model, not in the prompt.

Names are drifting again too. Elsbeth and Lotte are both **Vos**, which was Sanne Vos's surname in the run two back. "Sanne" itself is gone — that one *was* prompt-seeded and deleting the example killed it — but the surname carried over from the run history instead.

character_design_eval_ai.judge_notes:
The experiment returned a clean and useful answer: **the negative examples were load-bearing, the positive ones were mostly not, and one removal took a form spec with it by accident.**

**Negative examples: restore them.** The ban list — *no crashes, no falls, no fires, no machinery, no weather* — took deaths from five-in-six traffic accidents to zero in one version. Deleting it brought a car crash back in the very next run, with only the abstract chance test left standing. The abstract test is not sufficient on its own; the concrete fence is what did the work.

**Positive examples: keep them deleted.** Nothing got vaguer where it mattered. Occupations came back as "high school history teacher" and "hospital radiology technician" — plain and specific, with no examples to guide them. The sins, self-told versions and wants are all as strong as before. Two measured improvements arrived as well: pronouns about life people fell from 35 to 22 across the pair, the first real movement on that rule in four versions; and the pair is the most distinct in five runs.

**One removal was a mistake and should be reversed.** Along with the trait examples I stripped the phrase "usually a quality with a qualifier on it," which was a form specification, not an example. Both traits came back nominalised — "measured intensity", "quiet control" — where previous runs produced "Responsible but late" and "desperately capable". That clause should go back.

**One diagnosis of mine was wrong and is worth recording.** I attributed two leaks to prompt contamination. Deleting the examples settled it: "Sanne" disappeared completely, so that one genuinely was the prompt seeding itself. "Need to be needed" came back with the example gone, so that is a model prior and removing the text was never going to fix it. Half right.

**The prose field is the one real casualty.** Both paragraphs are now single comma-chained sentences — Rami's is 94 words with one full stop. The removed example was not offering content, it was demonstrating that the paragraph should be shaped by the life it describes. The facts inside are excellent and usable; the shape is an inventory. This field needs something back, but a *structural* instruction rather than a worked example.

**Net position.** Restore the death ban list and the trait form spec; leave the other seventeen positive examples deleted. That is the middle position this experiment was run to locate, and it now has evidence behind it rather than a guess.
